slides.say: A B C D is a square, and P is a point inside it, so that triangle B P C is equilateral. What is angle P A D?
at: A B C D is a square

slides.say: We need angle P A D, the small angle at A, between A P and the side A D. [short pause] We'll mark what each given tells us on the figure, and then use the triangle that holds the angle at A.
at: We need angle P A D

slides.say: [short pause] Where do we start? With the square. A square has lots of properties. All its sides are equal, and all its angles are ninety. Its diagonals are equal, they cut each other in half, they're perpendicular, and they cut the angles in half. We need to decide which of these matter here.

slides: There are no diagonals in this figure. P is inside the square, but it's not the point where the diagonals meet. So we probably won't need the diagonal properties.

slides.say: What we will need is this. All the sides are equal, so let's mark all four with the same little line. And all the angles are ninety. I'll mark the two that sit next to the angle we want, at B and at A. We may need them.
at: mark all four with the same little line

slides.say: Done with the square. The next given, B P C is equilateral. In an equilateral triangle all three sides are equal, B C, P C and B P. B C already has the mark, so P C and B P get the same mark. That's the catch in this question. The sides of the triangle are equal to the sides of the square. And all the angles of the triangle are sixty.
at: And all the angles of the triangle

slides.say: Now look at the triangle that holds the angle at A, triangle A B P. Two of its sides have the mark, B A and B P. So it's isosceles. If we hadn't marked the sides, we might not have noticed that.
at: Now look at the triangle that holds

slides.say: In an isosceles triangle, the angles across from the equal sides are equal. So angle B A P and angle B P A are equal. Let's call both of them alpha.
The angle at B, the top of this triangle, is ninety minus sixty, which is thirty.

The angles of a triangle add up to one hundred eighty. So thirty plus alpha plus alpha is one hundred eighty. Move the thirty across. One hundred eighty minus thirty is one hundred fifty, and that's two alpha. So one alpha is seventy-five.

Careful. Seventy-five is angle B A P, and seventy-five is choice number four. But the question asks for angle P A D. Angle B A P and angle P A D together fill the square's corner at A, which is ninety. So angle P A D is ninety minus seventy-five, which is fifteen. Choice number one is our answer. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
at: So angle P A D is ninety
Choice number one is our answer
